synth_text.title: Key Weighted‑Average Actuarial Assumptions (31 March)
synth_text.text:
The Group’s pension scheme liabilities are valued using the projected unit‑credit method, applying a set of principal actuarial assumptions that represent a weighted average of all individual schemes. As of 31 March, the weighted‑average assumptions are:

- **Rate of inflation:** 3.0 %  
- **Rate of increase in salaries:** 2.6 %  
- **Discount rate:** 2.6 %

These figures are used to project future pension payments and deferred revaluations, with the rate of pension increases directly linked to the inflation rate. The weighted‑average approach ensures that the assumptions reflect the overall characteristics of the Group’s diverse pension arrangements.

synth_text.title: Weighted Average Actuarial Assumptions for the Group’s Pension Schemes (31 March)
synth_text.text:
The Group’s pension scheme liabilities are measured using the projected unit‑credit method, applying the principal actuarial assumptions shown below. As of 31 March, the weighted‑average assumptions across all individual schemes are:

- **Rate of inflation:** 2.9 % (used to determine increases in pensions in payment and deferred revaluation)  
- **Rate of increase in salaries:** 2.7 %  
- **Discount rate:** 2.3 % to 2.5 % (reflecting a slight variation among schemes)

These figures represent a consolidated view of the assumptions applied to each scheme, ensuring a consistent basis for liability valuation. The inflation rate directly influences pension revaluation, while the salary growth rate and discount rate are used to project future benefit obligations and present‑value them appropriately.

header: Opening net book amount at 1 July 2017

text.value: 11 Intangible assets (continued)
(a) Intangible assets
RIGHTS AND LICENCES

Certain licences that NEXTDC possesses have an indefinite useful life and are carried at cost less impairment losses and are subject to impairment review at least annually and whenever there is an indication that it may be impaired.

Other licences that NEXTDC acquires are carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses. Amortisation is recognised on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life. The estimated useful life and amortisation method are reviewed at the end of each annual reporting period.
INTERNALLY GENERATED SOFTWARE

Internally developed software is capitalised at cost less accumulated amortisation. Amortisation is calculated using the straight-line basis over the asset’s useful economic life which is generally two to three years. Their useful lives and potential impairment are reviewed at the end of each financial year.
SOFTWARE UNDER DEVELOPMENT

Costs incurred in developing products or systems and costs incurred in acquiring software and licenses that will contribute to future period financial benefits through revenue generation and/or cost reduction are capitalised to software and systems. Costs capitalised include external direct costs of materials and services and employee costs.

Assets in the course of construction include only those costs directly attributable to the development phase and are only recognised following completion of technical feasibility and where the Group has an intention and ability to use the asset.

synth_text.title: NEXTDC Intangible Asset Movements – Summary for the Year Ended 30 June 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary outlines the movements in NEXTDC’s intangible assets for the financial year ended 30 June 2019, compared with the prior year (30 June 2018). The data are presented in thousands of Australian dollars ($'000) and are aligned with the company’s accounting policies for rights and licences, internally generated software, and software under development.

**1. Rights and Licences (Finite‑life licences)**  
- **Cost:** $104 k (unchanged)  
- **Accumulated amortisation:** $(91 k) (increased from $(48 k) in 2018)  
- **Net book amount (30 June 2019):** $13 k (down from $43 k at 1 July 2017)  

**Key movements**  
- Opening net book amount (1 July 2017): $43 k  
- Additions – externally acquired: $13 k  
- Amortisation charged during the year: $(43 k)  
- No internal transfers, re‑classifications or disposals were recorded.  

The net book value fell to $13 k after the sole addition was fully amortised during the year, reflecting the straight‑line amortisation approach applied to licences with a defined useful life.

**2. Internally Generated Software**  
- **Cost:** $9,555 k (up from $8,? k in 2018 – the table shows the current cost)  
- **Accumulated amortisation:** $(3,170 k) (up from $(1,424 k) in 2018)  
- **Net book amount (30 June 2019):** $7,381 k (up from $6,385 k in 2018)  

**Key movements**  
- Opening net book amount (1 July 2017): $442 k  
- Additions – externally acquired: – (none)  
- Additions – internally developed: – (none recorded this year)  
- Amortisation charged: $(1,746 k)  
- Transfers into this class: $7,563 k  
- Transfer between classes (re‑classification): $744 k  
- Disposals: $(618 k)  
- Closing net book amount (30 June 2019): $6,385 k  

The substantial increase in the net book amount is driven primarily by internal transfers of software assets into the “internally generated software” class, offset partially by disposals and amortisation. The straight‑line amortisation over an estimated useful life of two to three years, as described in the policy, is applied to these assets.

**3. Accounting Policy Highlights**  
- **Indefinite‑life licences** are carried at cost less impairment and are reviewed annually for impairment.  
- **Finite‑life licences** and **internally generated software** are amortised on a straight‑line basis over their estimated useful lives, with the useful life and amortisation method reviewed each reporting period.  
- **Software under development** costs are capitalised once technical feasibility is established and are subsequently amortised over the asset’s economic life.

**Conclusion**  
During the year ended 30 June 2019, NEXTDC’s intangible‑asset portfolio saw modest growth in cost and net book value, largely due to internal transfers of software assets. Amortisation continued to be applied consistently in line with the company’s policy of straight‑line allocation over the assets’ useful lives, while no new external acquisitions were made for the internally generated software category. The overall net book value of intangible assets increased, reflecting the company’s ongoing investment in software development and the re‑classification of existing assets.

synth_text.title: NEXTDC Intangible Asset Movements – Summary for the Year Ended 30 June 2019
synth_text.text:
**Overview**  
The following summary outlines the movements in NEXTDC’s intangible assets between 30 June 2018 and 30 June 2019, focusing on two distinct categories: (1) licences with indefinite useful lives (“Rights and licences”) and (2) internally generated software (“Software under development” and “Internally generated software”). All amounts are presented in thousands of Australian dollars ($'000).

---

### 1. Rights and licences (indefinite‑life assets)

| Item | 30 June 2018 | 30 June 2019 |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Opening net book amount (1 July 2017) | 8,053 | – |
| Additions – externally acquired | 5,253 | – |
| Additions – internally developed | 1,256 | – |
| Transfers out of the class | (7,563) | – |
| Disposals | (490) | – |
| **Closing net book amount** | 6,509 | 6,509 |
| **Cost of the class** | – | 6,509 |
| **Accumulated amortisation** | – | – |
| **Net book amount (cost less impairment)** | – | 16,284 |

**Key points**  
- These licences are carried at cost less impairment only; no amortisation is recorded.  
- The net book amount fell from $8,053 k to $6,509 k, mainly because of a large transfer out of the class ($7,563 k) and modest disposals ($490 k).  
- The cost of the class at 30 June 2019 is $6,509 k, giving a net book amount of $16,284 k after accounting for any impairment adjustments.

---

### 2. Internally generated software (finite‑life assets)

| Item | 30 June 2018 | 30 June 2019 |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| Opening net book amount (1 July 2017) | 8,538 | – |
| Additions – externally acquired | 5,266 | – |
| Additions – internally developed | 1,256 | – |
| Amortisation (straight‑line, 2‑3 yr life) | (1,789) | – |
| Transfer between classes (into software) | 744 | – |
| Disposals | (1,108) | – |
| **Closing net book amount** | 12,907 | 12,907 |
| **Cost of the class** | – | 16,168 |
| **Accumulated amortisation** | (3,261) | – |
| **Net book amount (cost less amortisation & impairment)** | – | 23,678 |

**Key points**  
- Software assets are amortised over an estimated economic life of two to three years on a straight‑line basis, as per the accounting policy.  
- The net book amount increased from $8,538 k to $12,907 k, driven by significant additions (external $5,266 k and internal $1,256 k) and a transfer into the class ($744 k).  
- Amortisation of $1,789 k and disposals of $1,108 k partially offset the additions.  
- At year‑end, the total cost of the software class is $16,168 k, with accumulated amortisation of $3,261 k, resulting in a net book amount of $23,678 k.

---

### 3. Interpretation in light of accounting policies  

- **Rights and licences**: Because many licences have an indefinite useful life, they are not amortised. Their carrying amount is reviewed annually for impairment only, which explains the absence of amortisation entries.  
- **Internally generated software**: These assets are capitalised once technical feasibility is established and are amortised over their useful economic life (2‑3 years). The straight‑line amortisation recorded aligns with the policy description.  

Overall, NEXTDC’s intangible asset portfolio shows a modest net increase in total net book value, primarily due to the growth of internally generated software, while the indefinite‑life licences experienced a net reduction because of transfers out of the class.

synth_text.title: Lifeway Net Sales Distribution by Dairy Category (Year Ended December 31)
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, Lifeway recorded total net sales of **$93.7 million**. The sales breakdown by product category is as follows:

| Category (as defined by Lifeway) | Net Sales (in $ thousands) | Share of Total Sales |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|
| **Drinkable Kefir (excluding ProBugs)** | $71,822 | **77 %** |
| **Cheese (European‑style soft cheeses, e.g., farmer cheese)** | $11,459 | **12 %** |
| **Cream and other (primarily cream, a kefir by‑product)** | $4,228 | **4 %** |
| **ProBugs Kefir (children’s kefir line)** | $2,780 | **3 %** |
| **Other Dairy (Cupped Kefir, Icelandic Skyr, etc.)** | $1,756 | **2 %** |
| **Frozen Kefir (soft‑serve and pint‑size containers, includes Kefir Shop sales)** | $1,617 | **2 %** |

**Key insights**

- **Drinkable Kefir dominates the portfolio**, contributing three‑quarters of total revenue. This category includes a wide range of organic and non‑organic kefir products, such as low‑fat, non‑fat, whole‑milk, protein‑enriched, and BioKefir varieties.
- **Cheese is the second‑largest segment**, accounting for roughly one‑tenth of sales and representing Lifeway’s European‑style soft cheese offerings.
- **Cream and other** products, largely derived as a by‑product of kefir production, generate a modest 4 % of sales.
- The **ProBugs line**, targeted at children, and **Frozen Kefir** each represent a small but strategic portion of the business (3 % and 2 % respectively).
- **Other Dairy** products, including Cupped Kefir and Icelandic Skyr, together contribute a minor 2 % of total revenue.

Overall, Lifeway’s sales are heavily concentrated in the core drinkable kefir segment, reflecting the company’s focus on cultured dairy beverages while maintaining a diversified portfolio of complementary dairy products.

synth_text.title: Lifeway Net Sales Breakdown by Dairy Product Category (Fiscal Year Ended December 31)
synth_text.text:
For the fiscal year ended December 31, Lifeway recorded total net sales of **$103.35 million**. Sales were distributed across six primary dairy product categories, each reflecting a distinct line of offerings:

- **Drinkable Kefir (excluding the ProBugs line)** generated the largest share, with **$78.5 million** in revenue, representing **76 %** of total sales. This category includes a wide range of organic and non‑organic kefir products—low‑fat, non‑fat, whole‑milk, protein‑enriched, and the BioKefir variant that adds extra probiotic cultures.
- **European‑style soft cheeses** contributed **$11.5 million** (11 %). These are farmer‑style cheeses sold in resealable cups.
- **Cream and other**—primarily the cream by‑product of kefir production—accounted for **$5.3 million** (5 %).
- **ProBugs Kefir**, the child‑focused kefir line, produced **$2.8 million** in sales (3 %).
- **Other dairy** products, which include Cupped Kefir and Icelandic Skyr (strained kefir and yogurt in resealable cups), added **$3.8 million** (4 %).
- **Frozen Kefir** (soft‑serve and pint‑size containers, including Lifeway Kefir Shop sales) contributed the smallest portion, **$1.4 million** (1 %).

All of Lifeway’s consolidated revenues stem from cultured dairy products manufactured using common processes and sold through a unified distribution network across the United States. The company reports a single segment, overseen by its chief operating decision makers (CEO, CFO, COO, and board chair). Sales are heavily concentrated among a few large retail customers—two major accounts together accounted for roughly 22 % of net sales, and the ten largest customers represented about 57 % of total revenue.

This breakdown underscores the pivotal role of drinkable kefir in Lifeway’s portfolio, while also highlighting the diversified yet smaller contributions from cheese, cream, child‑focused, other dairy, and frozen kefir offerings.
